title: Pain pathway: tooth → brain
topic: Why cold can give a sharp first pain and a dull second pain: Aδ vs C pulpal fibers, their relay to cortex, and convergence.

claims.claim: Two pulpal fibers, two speeds: Aδ myelinated (~5–30 m/s), C unmyelinated (~0.5–2 m/s)
claims.source: Range figures are the textbook fiber-class values (Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science; textbook, not a paper). Pulpal single-unit data consistent with them: Jyväsjärvi & Kniffki, J Physiol 1987;391:193-207 (PMID 3443945; cat intradental Aδ mean 13.9 m/s, range 3.6–26.0; C mean 1.3 m/s, range 0.5–2.2). Myelinated fast vs unmyelinated slow: Nair, Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 1995;80:710-9 (PMID 8680980)

claims.source: Närhi et al., Proc Finn Dent Soc 1992;88 Suppl 1:507-16 (PMID 1508908); Närhi et al., Arch Oral Biol 1994;39 Suppl:23S-30S (PMID 7702462)

claims.source: Byers & Närhi, Crit Rev Oral Biol Med 1999;10:4-39 (PMID 10759425); Sessle, Crit Rev Oral Biol Med 2000;11:57-91 (PMID 10682901); Sessle et al., Pain 1986;27:219-35 (PMID 3797017)

claims.claim: Synapse 2 in VPM thalamus → S1 face area; 1st pain is sharp, brief, well-localized
claims.source: Park et al., Brain Res 2006;1112:134-45 (PMID 16930568; tooth-pulp-driven nociceptive neurons in contralateral VPM, rat); Nair, Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 1995;80:710-9 (PMID 8680980); Ploner et al., PNAS 2002;99:12444-8 (PMID 12209003; first pain particularly related to S1)

claims.claim: In real teeth the dull pain lags by seconds, mostly the time for cold to reach the pulp
claims.source: Jyväsjärvi & Kniffki, J Physiol 1987;391:193-207 (PMID 3443945); Mengel et al., Pain 1993;55:159-69 (PMID 8309707)

claims.claim: 2nd pain is dull, aching, poorly localized; linked to S2 + cingulate
claims.source: Nair, Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 1995;80:710-9 (PMID 8680980); Ploner et al., PNAS 2002;99:12444-8 (PMID 12209003)

claims.claim: Partly diffuse because many inputs (teeth, skin, jaw muscle) converge on one caudalis neuron (animal data)
claims.source: Sessle et al., Pain 1986;27:219-35 (PMID 3797017)

claims.claim: Aδ: dentin stimuli (cold, air, probe); C: likely the ache of pulpitis; inflammation also sensitizes A fibers
claims.source: Närhi et al., Arch Oral Biol 1994;39 Suppl:23S-30S (PMID 7702462); Närhi et al., Proc Finn Dent Soc 1992;88 Suppl 1:507-16 (PMID 1508908)

claims.claim: Convergence in caudalis helps explain referred pain
claims.source: Sessle et al., Pain 1986;27:219-35 (PMID 3797017; cat caudalis, authors 'suggest a role' in spread and referral of pain); Basbaum et al., Cell 2009;139:267-84 (PMID 19837031; general principle: somatic–visceral convergence onto dorsal-horn WDR neurons 'likely contributes' to referred pain)

caption:
Sharp or dull? Two pulpal fibers, two speeds.

Aδ (myelinated, fast): brief, sharp, better-localized pain from dentin stimuli (cold, air, probe).
C (unmyelinated, slow): fire only once the stimulus reaches the pulp; likely the dull, diffuse ache of pulpitis. In real teeth the lag is seconds, mostly the time for cold to reach the pulp.
Inflammation sensitizes A fibers too: pain quality is a clue, not a diagnosis.
Convergence in caudalis helps explain referred pain (animal data).

Refs: Nair 1995, OOOOE · Närhi 1994, Arch Oral Biol · Jyväsjärvi 1987, J Physiol · Mengel 1993, Pain · Sessle 1986, Pain

title: Ibuprofen & COX: cuts new prostaglandins
topic: How ibuprofen reversibly plugs COX to cut new PGE₂, and why it can't erase prostaglandins already sensitising pulpal nerves.

claims.claim: Inflamed pulp frees arachidonic acid (PLA₂ cuts it from membrane phospholipids)
claims.source: Funk CD, Science 2001;294:1871-5 (PMID 11729303); pulp anchor (PGE₂ ↑ in inflamed pulp): Nakanishi T et al., J Endod 1995;21:131-6 (PMID 7561655)

claims.source: Smith WL et al., Annu Rev Biochem 2000;69:145-82 (PMID 10966456); Park JY et al., Clin Immunol 2006;119:229-40 (PMID 16540375)

claims.claim: COX-2 ↑ in inflamed pulp
claims.source: Nakanishi T et al., J Endod 2001;27:385-8 (PMID 11487130)

claims.claim: PGE₂ on nociceptor EP receptors lowers the firing threshold
claims.source: Kawabata A, Biol Pharm Bull 2011;34:1170-3 (PMID 21804201)

claims.claim: Ibuprofen reversibly (competitively) plugs the COX channel; one AA can slip through when it unbinds
claims.source: Selinsky BS et al., Biochemistry 2001;40:5172-80 (PMID 11318639); Orlando BJ et al., J Struct Biol 2015;189:62-6 (PMID 25463020)

claims.claim: Less new PGE₂ → nerve calms, but only partly (threshold recovers partway)
claims.source: Kawabata A, Biol Pharm Bull 2011;34:1170-3 (PMID 21804201); Nguyen V et al., J Endod 2020;46:1210-6 (PMID 32565333); Bowles WR et al., J Endod 2003;29:265-7 (PMID 12701777)

claims.claim: Other mediators (e.g. substance P) still act
claims.source: Bowles WR et al., J Endod 2003;29:265-7 (PMID 12701777)

claims.claim: Ibuprofen cuts NEW prostaglandins; it can't erase the ones already made
claims.source: Vane JR, Nat New Biol 1971;231:232-5 (PMID 5284360); Smith WL et al., Annu Rev Biochem 2000;69:145-82 (PMID 10966456); Selinsky BS et al., Biochemistry 2001;40:5172-80 (PMID 11318639); Nguyen V et al., J Endod 2020;46:1210-6 (PMID 32565333)

claims.claim: One rationale for dosing before treatment: pre-op NSAIDs aid IANB success; post-op pain benefit unclear
claims.source: Shirvani A et al., Clin Oral Investig 2017;21:43-52 (PMID 27837343); Nagendrababu V et al., J Endod 2018;44:914-922.e2 (PMID 29709297); de Geus JL et al., Eur Endod J 2018;3:123-33 (PMID 32161868)

claims.claim: PGE₂ counter, firing meter, threshold values and timing
claims.source: Toy model / schematic: toy counts, seeded stimulus bumps, time and size not to scale (labelled on screen)

caption:
What ibuprofen can't undo.

In inflamed pulp, COX (COX-2 up) turns arachidonic acid into PGE₂, which lowers the nerve's firing threshold.
Ibuprofen reversibly plugs the COX channel: less NEW PGE₂, not zero.
It can't erase what's already made, and other mediators (e.g. substance P) still act.
One rationale for dosing before treatment: pre-op NSAIDs aid IANB success in irreversible pulpitis; post-op pain benefit is unclear.

Refs: Vane 1971, Nat New Biol; Selinsky 2001, Biochemistry; Nakanishi 2001, J Endod; Kawabata 2011, Biol Pharm Bull; Bowles 2003, J Endod; Shirvani 2017, Clin Oral Investig; Nagendrababu 2018, J Endod; de Geus 2018, Eur Endod J; Nguyen 2020, J Endod

claims.claim: Steroid blocks cPLA₂ step, partly via annexin A1
claims.source: Croxtall et al., Biochem Pharmacol 1996;52:351-6 (PMID 8694860)

claims.claim: Steroid: less COX-2 made (COX-1 unaffected); NSAID blocks COX-1 & COX-2 enzyme activity
claims.source: Masferrer et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1994;270:1340-4 (PMID 7932188) [dex suppresses COX-2; COX-1 mRNA/protein unaffected]; Masferrer et al., PNAS 1994;91:3228-32 (PMID 8159730) [dex inhibits COX-2 expression; indomethacin = non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor]; Vane, Nat New Biol 1971;231:232-5 (PMID 5284360) [aspirin-like drugs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; predates the COX-1/COX-2 distinction]

claims.claim: Takeaway: acts upstream of NSAIDs, a gene-level brake on inflammation (on-screen sources line)
claims.source: Cain & Cidlowski, Nat Rev Immunol 2017;17:233-47 (PMID 28192415); Barnes, Br J Pharmacol 2006;148:245-54 (PMID 16604091); Abraham et al., J Exp Med 2006;203:1883-9 (PMID 16880258)

claims.claim: In endodontics, oral/injected steroids reduced post-op pain vs control at 6–24 h (29 RCTs, moderate certainty)
claims.source: Alajlan et al., J Endod 2024;50:724-34 (PMID 38490301)

claims.claim: Not a clinical ranking: steroids given only after treatment did not beat placebo for post-op pain
claims.source: Zanjir et al., J Endod 2020;46:1387-402 (PMID 32668310)

caption:
Why does dexamethasone's anti-inflammatory effect build over hours? It works on gene expression.

Dex enters the cell, binds the glucocorticoid receptor and enters the nucleus.
It turns anti-inflammatory genes up (annexin A1, MKP-1) and NF-κB/AP-1-driven genes down (COX-2, IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6).
So it acts upstream of where NSAIDs block COX (mechanism, not a clinical ranking).
In endo RCTs, systemic steroids cut post-op pain at 6–24 h (moderate certainty); post-op-only dosing didn't beat placebo.

Refs: Cain 2017, Nat Rev Immunol · Alajlan 2024, J Endod · Zanjir 2020, J Endod

claims.source: Ruggiero et al., J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022;80:920–43 (PMID 35300956)

claims.source: AAE Position Statement, Endodontic Implications of Bisphosphonate-Associated Osteonecrosis of the Jaws, 2010 (aae.org; not in PubMed); AAE Guideline, Endodontic Implications of Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw, 2018 (aae.org; not in PubMed); Ruggiero et al., J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022;80:920–43 (PMID 35300956); Moinzadeh et al., Int Endod J 2013;46:391–8 (PMID 23137312); clamp: Gallego et al., J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2011;69:e93–5 (PMID 21211886); over-instrumentation: Mauceri et al., BMC Oral Health 2025;25:1362 (PMID 40849463)

caption:
Patient on a bisphosphonate: extract or endo?

BPs bind bone mineral, get swallowed by resorbing osteoclasts and switch them off. Remodelling slows (not stops) and the drug stays in bone for years.
AAOMS 2022, MRONJ after extraction: 1.6–14.8% in cancer pts on BPs vs 0–0.15% in osteoporosis pts on BPs.
Restorable tooth + cancer-dose IV BP or denosumab: strongly prefer non-surgical RCT and minimise bone trauma. Never pause the drug without the prescriber.

Refs: Ruggiero 2022, J Oral Maxillofac Surg; Rogers 2011, Bone; AAE Position Statement 2010.

caption:
Metal vs fiber post: where does the stress go?

Many FEA models: stiff metal posts (≈4–11× dentin's modulus) concentrate dentin stress along the post–dentin interface; fiber posts load cervical dentin, like a natural tooth.
Lab overload: metal → more root fractures; fiber → more restorable failures. Clinically, root-fracture rates are similar.
A post retains the core; it doesn't reinforce the root. Ferrule + remaining dentin matter most.

Posterior tooth, ridge lost? Cover the cusps: onlay or crown.

caption:
Why does warm gutta-percha shrink? Follow its phases.

Most cones are β phase as supplied. Heat to ~42–49 °C and β converts to α; at ~53–59 °C it melts (amorphous) and flows under pressure.
On cooling it recrystallises (normal cooling gives β; only very slow cooling gives α) and contracts. It can keep shrinking for minutes–hours.
For warm techniques: keep plugger pressure on while it cools. Apical GP stays cooler (≲45 °C).

claims.claim: Tissue & dentin use it up → refresh often
claims.source: Macedo et al., Int Endod J 2010;43:1108-15 (PMID 20812947); Tejada et al., Int Endod J 2019;52:114-122 (PMID 30019752); Boutsioukis & Arias-Moliz, Int Endod J 2022;55 Suppl 3:588-612 (PMID 35338652); Cullen et al., J Endod 2015;41:920-4 (PMID 25791075)

caption:
Why does NaOCl in a canal need to be refreshed?
Unbuffered NaOCl (pH ~11–12) dissolves pulp tissue by reacting with it, and those reactions use it up.
Saponification and amino-acid neutralization consume hydroxide; chloramination and oxidation consume free chlorine (HOCl + OCl⁻).
Tissue and dentin deplete free chlorine at the interface, so exchange it often. Agitation and concentration matter too.

claims.claim: Proposed: nerve sprouting
claims.source: Byers MR et al., J Endod 1990;16:78-84 (PMID 2388022); Rodd HD & Boissonade FM, J Dent Res 2001;80:389-93 (PMID 11269734)

claims.claim: Lip numb ≠ pulp numb: IANB alone ~25–28% success in hot mandibular molars
claims.source: Fowler S et al., J Endod 2016;42:390-2 (PMID 26831048)

claims.claim: Plan B: buccal articaine infiltration, intraosseous, PDL, intrapulpal (supplemental success varies: articaine ~42–58%, IO ~88%); pre-op NSAID may also help
claims.source: Fowler S et al., J Endod 2016;42:390-2 (PMID 26831048); Matthews R et al., J Endod 2009;35:343-6 (PMID 19249592); Nusstein J et al., J Endod 1998;24:487-91 (PMID 9693577); Parirokh M & Abbott PV, Int Endod J 2022;55 Suppl 4:951-94 (PMID 35119117); pre-op NSAID: Pulikkotil SJ et al., Int Endod J 2018;51:989-1004 (PMID 29480930)

caption:
Hot tooth won't go numb? It's not just the acid.

Ion trapping is real: in acidic tissue, lidocaine (pKa ~7.7–7.9) has less base to cross the nerve membrane. That matters if you inject INTO infected tissue (abscess pus pH 6.0–7.3).
But an IANB is deposited far from the inflamed pulp. Proposed culprits: TTX-resistant Na+ channels, sensitized nerves, sprouting (mostly lab/animal data).
IANB alone: ~25–28% success in hot mandibular molars, even with a numb lip. Have a plan B.

Refs: Nekoofar 2009, IEJ; Roy & Narahashi 1992, J Neurosci; Fowler 2016, J Endod.

title: NiTi cyclic fatigue: why files snap in curves
topic: A file spinning in a curve flips its surface between tension and compression; strain ≈ d/(2R), so fatigue cracks grow until it snaps.

claims.claim: Why NiTi files snap in curves: cyclic fatigue is mechanism 1 of 2 (the other: torsion)
claims.source: Sattapan et al., J Endod 2000;26(3):161-5 (PMID 11199711); Parashos et al., J Endod 2004;30(10):722-5 (PMID 15448468)

claims.claim: Every turn in a curve = one tension–compression cycle at the file surface (rotating-bending)
claims.source: Li et al., J Endod 2002;28(6):448-51 (PMID 12067126); Pruett et al., J Endod 1997;23(2):77-85 (PMID 9220735); Cheung & Darvell, Int Endod J 2007;40(8):612-8 (PMID 17532775)

claims.claim: Peak surface strain ε ≈ d/(2R): tighter curve or thicker file → more strain
claims.source: Simple beam bending (outer-fibre strain), as used by Cheung & Darvell, Int Endod J 2007;40(8):612-8 (PMID 17532775); Pruett et al., J Endod 1997;23(2):77-85 (PMID 9220735); Haïkel et al., J Endod 1999;25(6):434-40 (PMID 10530246)

claims.claim: Example values: d 0.30 mm, R 5.0 mm → 3.0 %; R 3.0 mm → 5.0 %; d 0.36 mm → 6.0 %
claims.source: Toy model / schematic: arithmetic of ε = d/(2R) with example values (labelled 'example values' on screen)

claims.claim: Surface flaw → microcrack that grows every cycle; origin, striations, then overload dimples on the fracture face
claims.source: Anderson et al., J Endod 2007;33(10):1212-6 (PMID 17889692); Cheung & Darvell, Int Endod J 2007;40(8):619-25 (PMID 17511786)

claims.claim: The fatigue crack is microscopic, not visible clinically
claims.source: Cheung et al., Int Endod J 2005;38(11):802-9 (PMID 16218972); Cheung & Darvell, Int Endod J 2007;40(8):619-25 (PMID 17511786); Shen et al., J Endod 2006;32(1):61-5 (PMID 16410072)

claims.claim: Fatigue life used meter and fracture at N = 741 cycles
claims.source: Toy model / schematic: Miner's-rule damage sum with N_f ∝ ε^-2 (exponent from Cheung & Darvell 2007, PMID 17532775); labelled 'toy model · values illustrative' on screen

claims.claim: Then sudden fracture, often without warning; no unwinding first, unlike many torsional failures
claims.source: Sattapan et al., J Endod 2000;26(3):161-5 (PMID 11199711); Shen et al., J Endod 2006;32(1):61-5 (PMID 16410072)

claims.claim: Every turn in a curve spends fatigue life (above the ~0.7 % strain fatigue limit)
claims.source: Cheung & Darvell, Int Endod J 2007;40(8):612-8 (PMID 17532775)

caption:
Why do NiTi rotary files snap in curved canals? One big reason: cyclic fatigue.

Every turn in a curve flips the file's outer surface between tension and compression.
Surface strain ≈ d/(2R): a tighter curve or a thicker file means more strain per turn and fewer cycles to failure.
A microcrack starts at a surface flaw, grows each cycle, and the file can separate with no visible unwinding first. Torsion is the other mechanism, and clinically the two often combine.

Refs: Pruett 1997, J Endod; Cheung & Darvell 2007, Int Endod J (Parts 1-2); Shen 2006, J Endod; Sattapan 2000, J Endod

topic: Periapical bone loss from canal bacteria can be under way while a 2-D PA still looks normal; CBCT and histology find more lesions.

claims.source: Chang et al., J Endod 2020;46:496-501 (PMID 32057449)

claims.source: AAE & AAOMR Joint Position Statement, Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol 2015;120:508-12 (PMID 26346911)

claims.source: Ørstavik, Int Endod J 1996;29:150-5 (PMID 9206419)

caption:
A normal PA doesn't mean no lesion.

Canal bacteria trigger the host response: immune cells, IL-1β/TNF-α/PGE₂ and a rising RANKL:OPG ratio drive osteoclastic bone loss.
A small lesion in cancellous bone can stay quiet on a 2-D film. PDL widening may be the first hint; the radiolucency gets much clearer as it grows and reaches the cortex.
83 dog roots vs histology: PA 71%, CBCT 84%, histology 93%.
PA stays first-line; consider limited-FOV CBCT when signs don't add up.

topic: How cold pulls fluid outward through open dentinal tubules to fire pulpal A-fibres, and why occluding tubules (flow ∝ r⁴) quiets it.

claims.claim: Dentine is riddled with fluid-filled tubules

claims.source: Toy model / schematic: Hagen-Poiseuille at same pressure, laminar flow; applied to dentine by Pashley DH, J Endod 1986;12:465-74 (PMID 3465852) and Prati C, J Dent 1994;22:83-8 (PMID 8195480: small changes in functional tubule diameter greatly modify permeability, per Poiseuille-Hagen)

claims.claim: Seal the tubules, still the fluid: the logic behind tubule-occluding desensitisers

claims.source: Liu X-X et al., BMC Oral Health 2020;20:220 (PMID 32762733: hydrodynamic theory widely accepted, mechanisms still unclear); Bernal L et al., Sci Adv 2021;7:eabf5567 (PMID 33771873)

caption:
Why does an iced drink zap a sensitive tooth?

Cold, air and sugar pull fluid outward through open tubules; the flow tugs A-fibre endings at the pulp–dentine border → sharp pain (hydrodynamic theory).
Poiseuille: flow ∝ r⁴, so narrowed tubules still the fluid: the logic behind occluding desensitisers.
Leading model, not the whole story (odontoblast TRPC5 may sense cold directly). DH is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out caries, cracks, pulpitis.

claims.claim: mA -> how many: more electrons, more photons, same energies (4 -> 8 mA, values illustrative)
claims.source: Seibert JA. J Nucl Med Technol 2004;32(3):139-47 (PMID 15347692) - full text: a larger filament current releases more electrons; McCollough CH. Radiographics 1997;17(4):967-84 (PMID 9225393) - abstract: quantity proportional to tube current; spectrum shape depends on anode material, tube potential, filtration and waveform (not on tube current)

claims.claim: kVp -> how hard: max keV = kVp (60 -> 70 kVp, values illustrative); electrons drawn faster with a bigger impact flash
claims.source: Seibert JA. J Nucl Med Technol 2004;32(3):139-47 (PMID 15347692) - full text: electron kinetic energy (keV) = tube voltage; maximum X-ray energy (keV) set by the peak voltage (kVp)

claims.claim: kVp -> + how many: output ~ kVp squared, i.e. tube output (exposure / air kerma at the port) rises roughly with the square of kVp; electron count unchanged
claims.source: McCollough CH. Radiographics 1997;17(4):967-84 (PMID 9225393) - abstract; Nickoloff EL, Berman HL. Radiographics 1993;13(6):1337-48 (PMID 8290728) - abstract: output increases by approximately the square of the tube potential

claims.claim: kVp up: less image contrast (swatch change exaggerated and drawn density-matched: object tones compress, the directly exposed background stays black)
claims.source: European Commission. Radiation Protection 136: European guidelines on radiation protection in dental radiology. 2004, sect. 4.1 - guideline full text. At unchanged mAs the real image would also be darker. Caveat: 60 vs 70 kVp had minimal effect on CMOS sensors in one phantom study (Pita de Melo D et al. Dentomaxillofac Radiol 2026, PMID 42538829 - abstract)

claims.claim: Time -> how long: same beam, on longer; mAs = mA x s (0.10 s -> 0.80 mAs, 0.20 s -> 1.60 mAs at 8 mA; values illustrative, slow motion)
claims.source: McCollough CH. Radiographics 1997;17(4):967-84 (PMID 9225393) - abstract: quantity proportional to exposure time; Seibert 2004 (PMID 15347692) - full text: mAs

claims.claim: Cheat sheet: mA -> how many (same energies); kVp -> how hard + how many (max keV = kVp, output ~ kVp squared); time -> how long (mAs = mA x s)
claims.source: McCollough 1997, Radiographics (PMID 9225393); Seibert 2004, J Nucl Med Technol (PMID 15347692). On-screen source line: McCollough; Zink, Radiographics 1997 - Seibert, J Nucl Med Technol 2004 - values illustrative

caption:
3 knobs. What does each do inside the X-ray tube?
mA = how many: hotter filament, more electrons, more photons, same energies.
kVp = how hard: max photon energy (keV) = kVp, and tube output rises roughly with kVp². Higher kVp = less contrast (minimal for 60 vs 70 kVp on CMOS sensors in one phantom study).
Time = how long: same beam, on longer. mAs = mA × s. Many intraoral units fix kV or nearly so; time is the main control.
~99% of the energy becomes heat.
Schematic; settings illustrative.
Refs: McCollough 1997, Zink 1997, Radiographics; Seibert 2004, J Nucl Med Technol; EC RP136 2004; Pita de Melo 2026, Dentomaxillofac Radiol

claims.source: Siqueira JF Jr & Rôças IN, J Oral Microbiol 2009;1 (doi:10.3402/jom.v1i0.2009; PMID 21523208; full text), text and Table 1; a review-level range of study means ('a mean of 10-20 species/phylotypes'), not the range of single canals

claims.source: Mostly Gram-positive after instrumentation/medication: Siqueira JF Jr & Rôças IN, J Endod 2008;34:1291-1301.e3 (PMID 18928835; abstract: 'gram-positive bacteria are the most dominant'); fewer species and cells after treatment: Siqueira JF Jr & Rôças IN, J Oral Microbiol 2009;1 (PMID 21523208; full text); no number shown

claims.claim: PERSISTENT / SECONDARY (previously treated tooth): 1-5 taxa per canal (adequately treated; culture + PCR)

'Often found' = prevalence 24-77 % in the wider literature: Stuart CH et al., J Endod 2006;32:93-8 (PMID 16427453; abstract)

claims.claim: Primary: mostly obligate anaerobes, Gram - and +
claims.source: Figdor D & Sundqvist G, Aust Dent J 2007;52(1 Suppl):S38-51 (PMID 17546861; abstract); Byström A & Sundqvist G, Scand J Dent Res 1981;89:321-8 (PMID 6947391; abstract)

claims.claim: Persistent/secondary: more facultatives, mostly Gram + (culture and targeted PCR findings), sometimes yeast
claims.source: Pinheiro ET et al., Int Endod J 2003;36:1-11 (PMID 12656508; abstract); Molander A et al., Int Endod J 1998;31:1-7 (PMID 9823122; abstract); Siqueira JF Jr & Rôças IN, J Oral Microbiol 2009;1 (doi:10.3402/jom.v1i0.2009; PMID 21523208; full text), Table 1. Yeast: Siqueira & Rôças 2009 (up to 18 % of treated teeth, narrative review); pooled prevalence 8.2 % across all infection types, Mergoni G et al., J Endod 2018;44:1616-1625.e9 (PMID 30241680; abstract); no difference by infection type in Persoon IF et al., Int Endod J 2017;50:1055-66 (PMID 27987307; abstract)

claims.claim: PERSISTENT: survived treatment. SECONDARY: got in during or after treatment
claims.source: Siqueira JF Jr & Rôças IN, J Oral Microbiol 2009;1 (doi:10.3402/jom.v1i0.2009; PMID 21523208; full text)

claims.claim: Sequencing finds more taxa in both
claims.source: Treated teeth: Siqueira JF Jr et al., PLoS One 2016;11:e0162887 (PMID 27689802; full text: mean 116 OTUs per root apex, 'substantially larger bacterial richness per tooth'); primary: Santos AL et al., PLoS One 2011;6:e28088 (PMID 22132218; full text: mean 71 OTUs per chronic case, 'much higher than previously reported'); both types 'highly diverse' by sequencing: Manoil D et al., Proteomics Clin Appl 2020;14:e1900060 (PMID 31950679; abstract). OTUs are not species

claims.claim: Which cards are dealt, how many survive the sweep, card order, the all-Gram-positive right-hand hand and the pip meters
claims.source: Toy model / schematic: labelled on screen 'schematic decks'; icons are textbook morphology, not to scale. Gram-negative anaerobes also occur in treated teeth (F. nucleatum in 10 of 42, Rôças & Siqueira 2012); the right hand shows none

caption:
Who lives in the canal? Depends on whether the tooth was treated.

Primary (untreated necrotic pulp): ~10-20 taxa per canal (molecular studies), mostly anaerobes, Gram - and +.
Root-filled, with a lesion: 1-5 taxa if adequately treated (culture, early PCR), more facultatives, mostly Gram +, sometimes yeast.
Persistent = survived treatment; secondary = got in during or after it.
E. faecalis: qPCR, 11 of 29 such teeth, dominant in 1. Sequencing finds more taxa in both.

Refs: Siqueira & Rôças 2009, J Oral Microbiol; Rôças & Siqueira 2012, J Clin Microbiol; Siqueira 2016, PLoS One; Manoil 2020, Proteomics Clin Appl

title: Working length & apical size: the evidence
topic: What outcome studies say about stopping 0–2 mm short of the radiographic apex and about apical size, and how weak the evidence is.

claims.claim: Toy model / schematic: apex sketch labeled radiographic apex, major foramen (opening on the side, off the root tip), minor constriction, CDJ; 'schematic / not to scale'
claims.source: Standard textbook terminology for the labels (Cohen's Pathways of the Pulp, 11th ed., Hargreaves & Berman, eds., Elsevier 2016; cited as a textbook, not re-read; no number taken from it). Off-tip foramen: Martos et al., Int Endod J 2009;42:329-34 (PMID 19220517; abstract: major foramen at the root tip in 40% of teeth). A constriction is often absent: Wu, Wesselink & Walton, Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 2000;89:99-103 (PMID 10630950; abstract; narrative review)

claims.claim: Green zone 0–2 mm short of the radiographic apex; slips 94% '0–2 mm short' · 76% 'long' (red scribble drawn out of the foramen and past the dashed 0 line = beyond the radiographic apex) · 68% '>2 mm short' — 'healed · necrotic + lesion · 8–10 yr'
claims.source: Sjögren et al., J Endod 1990;16:498-504 (PMID 2084204). PubMed abstract gives the design (356 patients, 8-10 yr), 86% healing with necrosis + radiolucency, and that the level of the root filling significantly affected outcome. The 94/76/68 breakdown is full-text data: primary full text not accessible; confirmed by secondary quotation in an open-access paper (Tarim Ertas et al., ScientificWorldJournal 2013;2013:514841, PMID 23431255, PMC3574741; full text re-read in the citation audit) and consistent with a review abstract (Wu et al. 2000, PMID 10630950: infected canals about 20% lower success when >2 mm short or past the apex than at 0-2 mm). Check against the paper's results table before posting. Unit = roots; one Swedish cohort

claims.claim: per mm short ~12–14% worse odds
claims.source: Two cohorts with different metrics, hence 'worse'. Chugal et al., Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 2003;96:81-90 (PMID 12847449; abstract: in teeth/roots with apical periodontitis each mm of working length lost raised the chance of failure by 14%; measured from the radiographic apex; 4 yr). Ng et al., Int Endod J 2011;44:583-609 (PMID 21366626; not in the abstract; primary full text read by the fact-checker and again in the citation audit: odds of success reduced by 12%, OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.97, for every un-instrumented mm short of the apex-locator zero; the paper's final-model table prints OR 0.87; primary and retreatment roots pooled, 2-4 yr)

claims.claim: <#30 vs ≥#30: 'irrigant reaches apical third (in vitro)'; 'debris' left in the smaller preparation
claims.source: Khademi et al., J Endod 2006;32:417-20 (PMID 16631839; abstract: SEM of debris and smear layer in the apical third of 40 mesiobuccal canals of extracted mandibular first molars, master apical file #20/25/30/35; minimum size #30 for penetration of irrigants to the apical third; irrigation protocol not given in the abstract). Toy model / schematic: the flow lines and specks are drawn, not simulated; consistent with Boutsioukis & Gutierrez Nova, J Endod 2021;47:1487-95 (PMID 34118256; abstract; computational fluid dynamics: irrigant did not reach working length at 20 or 25/.06, did at 30/.06 with a 30-G open-ended needle). Depends on taper and needle

claims.claim: RCT · healed at 12 mo: binding file +2 → 48%; +3 or more → 71–92%
claims.source: Saini et al., J Endod 2012;38:1309-15 (PMID 22980168; abstract: 48%, 71.43%, 80%, 84.61%, 92% for 2-6 sizes past the first apical binding file; mandibular first molars; 129 evaluated at 12 months; only +2 significantly worse, +3 to +6 not different from each other)

claims.claim: Summary 1: Infected: fill 0–2 mm short of x-ray apex
claims.source: Sjögren 1990 (PMID 2084204) as above: level of the root filling relative to the radiographic apex. Limited to infected roots because in Chugal 2003 (PMID 12847449; abstract) teeth with a normal pulp and periapex showed the reverse: successes ended 1.23 mm and failures 0.20 mm short of the radiographic apex

claims.claim: Summary 2: Binding file +3 sizes beat +2
claims.source: Saini 2012 (PMID 22980168) as above. Second RCT: Fatima et al., J Endod 2021;47:1345-51 (PMID 34058250; abstract): +2 sizes with a 4% taper had the lowest success (57.1%) and differed significantly from the other three groups (+2 with 6% taper, +3 with 4% or 6%). The first binding file is a poor gauge of apical diameter (Wu et al., Int Endod J 2002;35:264-7, PMID 11985678; abstract; 20 curved mandibular premolars)

claims.claim: Evidence: LOW · cohorts · in vitro · small RCTs
claims.source: Descriptive tag. A published 'low' rating exists for apical size and healing only: Sabeti et al., J Endod 2024;50:292-8 (PMID 38135112; abstract: 2 studies, overall quality of evidence low). The working-length data are observational cohorts and were not formally graded

caption:
Where to stop, and how big? The evidence on one board.

WHERE: necrotic pulp + lesion, per root, 8–10 yr, one cohort: 94% healed when filled 0–2 mm short of the radiographic apex, 76% long, 68% >2 mm short. Two more cohorts: about 12–14% worse odds per mm short. Normal pulp/periapex: trend reversed.

HOW BIG: in vitro, irrigant reached the apical third from ~#30. An RCT (mandibular molars, 12 mo): binding file +2 healed 48%, +3 to +6 71–92%; only +2 was significantly worse.

Evidence: low. Schematic animation.

Refs: Sjögren 1990, Khademi 2006, Saini 2012, Sabeti 2024 (J Endod); Chugal 2003 (OOOOE); Ng 2011 (Int Endod J).

title: The separated file: case notes
topic: Why NiTi files separate (torsion vs fatigue), the risk factors, prevention, and what a retained fragment means.

claims.claim: Two mechanisms: TORSION (tip binds, shaft turns; may unwind) and FATIGUE (flexing in a curve; often no warning)
claims.source: Two modes: Sattapan et al., J Endod 2000;26:161-5 (PMID 11199711, abstract). Definitions, unwinding, and fatigue typically without macroscopic warning signs: Ohri et al., Materials (Basel) 2024;17:6147 (PMID 39769746, PMC full text, narrative review). Fracture without visible deformation in 73.9% of failed ProTaper files, attributed by its authors to overload rather than fatigue: Spanaki-Voreadi et al., Int Endod J 2006;39:171-8 (PMID 16507069, abstract)

claims.claim: Toy model / schematic: both mechanism animations and the radiograph (labelled 'schematic')
claims.source: Schematic; fracture at mid-curve after Pruett et al., J Endod 1997;23:77-85 (PMID 9220735)

claims.claim: Risk factors: tight curve, big file (both = cyclic fatigue in a curve, in vitro; source line on both cards)
claims.source: Pruett et al., J Endod 1997;23:77-85 (PMID 9220735)

claims.claim: Risk factors: no glide path, forced, reuse
claims.source: Berutti et al., J Endod 2004;30:228-30 (PMID 15085052, in vitro); Sattapan et al., J Endod 2000;26:161-5 (PMID 11199711, authors' inference); Gomes et al., Aust Endod J 2021;47:372-85 (PMID 33410578)

claims.claim: Operator ringed: most important influence on defect rates (unwinding or fracture) among the factors studied, 14 endodontists
claims.source: Parashos et al., J Endod 2004;30:722-5 (PMID 15448468)

claims.claim: Prevention: glide path (Berutti 2004, in vitro), light touch, discard early
claims.source: Glide path: Berutti et al., J Endod 2004;30:228-30 (PMID 15085052). Light touch: expert opinion (Fan et al., Int J Oral Sci 2025;17:46, PMID 40484859). Discard early: Shen et al., J Endod 2009;35:193-6 (PMID 19166771); Gomes et al., Aust Endod J 2021;47:372-85 (PMID 33410578)

claims.claim: Healed, >= 1 yr: fragment 91.8% vs control 94.5%, n.s. (146 matched pairs)
claims.source: Spili et al., J Endod 2005;31:845-50 (PMID 16306815)

claims.claim: Removed or bypassed, by curve: before 100%, beyond 31% (at the curve 60%; 72 teeth in total, subgroup sizes not in the abstract)
claims.source: Shen et al., Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol Endod 2004;98:605-10 (PMID 15529134)

claims.claim: Bypass / retrieve / leave + monitor (three options, no guideline, case-based); infection drives the outcome
claims.source: Madarati et al., J Endod 2013;39:569-81 (PMID 23611371); Lin et al., J Am Dent Assoc 2005;136:187-93 (PMID 15782522, expert statement)

caption:
Case notes: the separated file.
Torsion, fatigue or both; often no visible warning. Operator: biggest influence on defects (unwinding or fracture; 14 endodontists). Curve, size, glide path: in vitro.
Fragment left: healed 91.8% vs 94.5% matched controls, n.s. (146 pairs, ≥1 yr, specialists). Removed or bypassed: all before the curve, 60% at it, 31% beyond (72 teeth, mixed techniques, 2004). A fragment can block cleaning; infection drives the outcome.
Schematic animation.
Refs: Sattapan 2000, Parashos 2004, Pruett 1997, Berutti 2004, Spili 2005 (J Endod); Spanaki-Voreadi 2006 (IEJ); Shen 2004 (OOOOE); Lin 2005 (JADA); Ohri 2024 (Materials).

title: Bioceramics: bactericidal or bacteriostatic?
topic: In vitro, fresh calcium silicate sealer kills on contact and set MTA only partially, fading with aging; clinical healing is comparable.

claims.claim: MTA: pH 10.2 at mixing, 12.5 at 3 h (cement, pH meter)
claims.source: Torabinejad et al., J Endod 1995;21:349-53 (PMID 7499973), abstract

claims.claim: Schematic: pink pH halo, hydroxyl-ion dots and the agar zone on the fresh plate (a zone = no growth, not kill)
claims.source: Illustration; calcium silicate materials can give agar zones: Biodentine immediately after mixing, Farrugia et al., J Appl Biomater Funct Mater 2017;15:e153-61 (PMID 28256700); EndoSequence BC Sealer, 6.00 mm zone read at 48 h, Candeiro et al., Int Endod J 2016;49:858-64 (PMID 26281002); abstracts

claims.claim: Fresh iRoot SP: all free-floating E. faecalis dead in 2 min (direct contact test, in vitro)
claims.source: Zhang et al., J Endod 2009;35:1051-5 (PMID 19567333), abstract

claims.claim: Set: partial, fading. Set ProRoot MTA aged in water, 1 h contact with E. faecalis: 97% killed at day 1, 82% at day 7 of aging (in vitro)
claims.source: Farrugia et al., Sci Rep 2017;7:41359 (PMID 28128328), full text (PMC5269669): percentages 97.30% and 81.76% in the Discussion; log10 counts in Table 1

claims.claim: Set plate shows no clear zone (set ProRoot MTA gave no inhibition zone); residual halo schematic
claims.source: Farrugia et al., Sci Rep 2017;7:41359 (PMID 28128328), full text

claims.claim: In dentin tubules, sealers: slow, partial kill; more dead at day 30 than day 1 (in vitro; cell counts schematic)
claims.source: Wang et al., J Endod 2014;40:505-8 (PMID 24666900); Du et al., J Endod 2015;41:1294-8 (PMID 26092772), abstracts

claims.claim: Bactericidal = count falls; bacteriostatic = count held (schematic curves and colonies)
claims.source: Definition and time-kill curve shapes: Ishak et al., J Antimicrob Chemother 2025;80:1-17 (PMID 39471409), full text (PMC11695898). Laboratory, condition-dependent label: Pankey & Sabath, Clin Infect Dis 2004;38:864-70 (PMID 14999632), abstract

claims.claim: FRESH and SET both sit on the bactericidal half; set = partial kill (under 2 log in 1 h); bacteriostatic action has not been measured
claims.source: Inference from Zhang 2009 (PMID 19567333) and Farrugia 2017 (PMID 28128328)

claims.claim: Verdict: Fresh: bactericidal on contact; Set: partial, fades (both tagged IN VITRO)
claims.source: Zhang et al., J Endod 2009 (PMID 19567333), abstract; Farrugia et al., Sci Rep 2017 (PMID 28128328), full text

claims.claim: Healing: comparable (tagged CLINICAL; single-cone trials vs other sealers: single cone + calcium silicate sealer vs other sealers/techniques, 3 trials, failure RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.33-1.51, NS)
claims.source: Sabeti et al., J Endod 2024;50:735-46.e1 (PMID 38548045), abstract; see also Donnermeyer et al., J Dent 2026;176:107002 (PMID 42668107), abstract

caption:
Bioceramics: bactericidal or bacteriostatic? It depends on when, and on the test.
• Fresh iRoot SP killed all free-floating E. faecalis in 2 min of contact (AH Plus: 5); pH alone did not explain it.
• Set ProRoot MTA, 1 h contact: 97% killed after 1 day in water, 82% after 7 (<2 log); aged in blood, no effect by day 7.
• In tubules, sealers kill slowly and partially (BC Sealer = AH Plus).
• Clinical: healing similar to other sealers (single-cone trials).
In vitro unless stated. Schematic: halo, agar zone (no growth, not kill), counts, curves.
Refs: Zhang 2009, Wang 2014, Du 2015, Sabeti 2024 (J Endod); Farrugia 2017 (Sci Rep).

claims.claim: BIOCOMPATIBLE · early inflammation subsides (animal histology)
claims.source: Torabinejad & Parirokh, J Endod 2010;36:190-202 (PMID 20113774); Gomes-Filho et al., J Endod 2009;35:256-60 (PMID 19166785); Moretton et al., J Biomed Mater Res 2000;52:528-33 (PMID 11007621): subsided to 'mostly moderate' under rat skin; abstracts

claims.source: Albrektsson & Johansson, Eur Spine J 2001;10 Suppl 2:S96-101 (PMID 11716023); abstract: recruitment of immature cells and their stimulation to develop into preosteoblasts

claims.claim: Verdict (MTA-type calcium silicate cements): BIOCOMPATIBLE ✓ tissue tolerates it (animal + human histology) · OSTEOCONDUCTIVE ✓ bone grows on it (animal histology)

caption:
Are endodontic bioceramics osteoinductive? Depends on the definition.
Biocompatible: yes. Cementum covered MTA in 5 of 6 monkey root ends, 5 months (amalgam: none).
Osteoconductive: yes. Bone forms directly on MTA in bone.
Osteoinductive: in culture BMP-2 (PDL cells), ALP, osteocalcin (marrow cells) rise. Strict test, bone at a non-bony site: not shown. Under rat skin: mineral, no bone; rats are a weak model, no large-animal test found.
Mostly MTA data. Schematic animation.
Refs: Albrektsson 2001 Eur Spine J; Barradas 2011 Eur Cell Mater; Torabinejad 1997, 1998, Maeda 2010 J Endod; Wang 2014 Cell Prolif; Moretton 2000 J Biomed Mater Res.
